newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen steady to up at open, awaits data.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen steady to up at open, awaits data.

text.p: Wall Street stocks were expected to open steady to slightly higher on Monday, with personal income and consumption data giving the markets some initial direction on the final day of the fiscal quarter.
The Chicago Purchasing Manager's Index for June, due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, should also draw attention, analysts said.
But the recently-volatile stock market is expected to then shift its focus to a meeting of key Federal Reserve policy makers which starts tomorrow, they said.
"Barring a surprise in the personal income and consumption data, we could hold steady until tomorrow," Pierre Ellis, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics, said.
In early trade, the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index was up 1.35 points at 898.25.
On Friday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average finished a week of wild swings by closing up around 33 points at 7688.

Personal income for May was forecast to rise 0.4 percent compared with a 0.1 percent rise in April, while consumption was expected to rise 0.3 percent in May versus a previous 0.1 percent increase. Both data were due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
"Periodically, something happens to the consumption number which might change everybody's thinking about second quarter GDP (gross domestic product)," Ellis said.
While consumption data would shed light on demand, analysts said the Chicago Purchasing Managers Index would be watched for insight into the manufacturing sector.

"This could be the most important report of the day, because it will give us some sort of clue about the NAPM report, which comes out tomorrow," Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said.
The Chicago Purchasing Managers Index was expected to show a reading of 57.5 in June compared with 56.8 reading in April.
The National Association of Purchasing Managers Index, due out tomorrow, was expected to show a reading of 56.4 compared with 57.1 in April.
After early activity, traders will look to the Federal Open Market Committee meeting, which starts tomorrow, and Thursday's key employment report for June, analysts said.
The Federal Reserve will meet for two days and was seen announcing any interest rate decision on Wednesday. Most analysts said they expected it to leave rates unchanged.
Japan's Nikkei average closed up 81.21 points at 20,604.96, as robust demand erased earlier losses.
In London, the FTSE 100 was off 0.8 points at 4639.5. U.S. stocks there were steady to marginally higher in quiet trade.
The dollar was at session lows versus the yen in Tokyo, after trimming its earlier gains on long liquidation and sales by Japanese exporters, traders said.
It was trading at 114.28/33 yen in Tokyo and at 1.7437/47 marks in Europe. In Europe, the dollar was off highs after pushing to a 40-month peak of 1.7465 marks.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that Microsoft Corp should be wary of how it spends its cash, learning from International Business Machines Corp, which squandered some money in the 1980s.
The New York Times said in a news analysis piece that AT&T Corp must now regroup and devise a strategy to compete on its own, after merger talks with SBC Communications Corp were suspended.
